tracked_topics.full_content:
--- Page 1 ---
Policy Brief 1 of 2026 
RESEARCH DEPARTMENT 
The Role of the Security Sector in Climate Change Adaptation and Disaster Response in 
Zimbabwe: A Framework for Civil-Military Coordination 
 
 
Chimanikire Soccicah (Researcher) 
 
Executive Summary 
Climate-induced disasters, cyclones, floods, and droughts are increasingly becoming non-
traditional security threats in Zimbabwe. These threats undermine national stability, food 
security, and public safety. Zimbabwe currently lacks a binding legal framework to formally 
integrate the security sector into disaster management although they are often engaged in 
disaster management. Cabinet endorsed the National Multi-Hazard Contingency Plan 
(2025/2026) in December 2025, formally integrating the Zimbabwe Defence Forces (ZDF) 
into disaster management. The plan lacks the legislative force. While the ZDF has introduced 
advanced training and maintains air mobility assets, serious implementation gaps remain: 
resource constraints, over-centralisation in Harare, and concerns that military deployment may 
lean toward enforcement rather than humanitarian support. Drawing on regional models from 
Mozambique, Malawi, and South Africa, this brief advocates for urgent legislative and 
operational reforms, chief among them the enactment of the new Disaster Risk Management 
and Civil Protection Bill, mandated training for police and prison services, dedicated 
engineering and air mobility units, binding standard operating procedures, a joint civil-military 
coordination centre, and contingency funding, to transform the security sector into a 
predictable, accountable partner in climate adaptation while safeguarding civilian authority.

--- Page 2 ---
1.0 Introduction 
Zimbabwe faces escalating climate-related hazards. Cyclone Idai (2019) claimed over 300 
lives, displaced thousands and caused more than USD 600 million in damages. The 2023–2024 
El Niño-induced drought reduced maize harvests by 60 per cent, threatening food security for 
over 7 million rural inhabitants. In response, the government adopted the National 
Multi-Hazard Contingency Plan (2025/2026) in December 2025, formally activating the ZDF’s 
role in responding to projected floods, severe storms and droughts. Drawing lessons from Idai, 
the plan shifts from a purely reactive, top-down approach to a proactive model, with the 
military playing key roles in search and rescue, logistics and disaster risk management training. 
Advanced technologies are being piloted: drone-based mapping of high-risk areas, satellite 
early warning systems and blockchain-based aid distribution to reduce corruption and delays. 
Regional cooperation through the SADC Humanitarian and Emergency Operations Centre is 
also strengthening. 
Despite these advances, major obstacles continue to hamper progress. The current response 
system is marked by high-level policy centralisation in Harare and persistent resource 
shortages. There are also concerns about the securitisation of disaster management, particularly 
when military deployment involves enforcement measures. Past experiences, such as during 
the COVID-19 pandemic, indicate that military involvement may sometimes lead to punitive, 
enforcement-oriented approaches rather than community-based protection. It is important to 
distinguish between such enforcement roles and humanitarian support functions like search and 
rescue or logistics, which raise fewer human rights concerns. Addressing these gaps requires a 
deliberate policy framework that builds on the 2025/2026 Contingency Plan by adding 
legislative backing, binding protocols and modern technology integration. 
2.0 Background 
Zimbabwe’s vulnerability to climate-induced disasters is acute. The Civil Protection Act 
(Chapter 10:06) establishes the Department of Civil Protection (DCP) under the Ministry of 
Local Government and Public Works as the lead disaster agency, yet the DCP lacks sufficient 
logistical capacity, personnel and rapid reach capabilities. A new National Disaster 
Management Centre is nearing completion, which should improve coordination, but the DCP 
itself estimates that USD 300 million is required for full capacitation. As a result, the Zimbabwe 
Defence Forces (ZDF), the Zimbabwe Republic Police and the Zimbabwe Prison and 
Correctional Services are routinely deployed. The 2025/2026 National Multi-Hazard 
Contingency Plan now formally integrates the ZDF as a key operational partner within the 
National Civil Protection Committee, alongside police, non-governmental organisations and 
relevant line ministries. 
The ZDF has made significant progress in disaster training. The Zimbabwe National Defence 
University offers a Master of Science Degree in Disaster Management, and the ZDF unveiled 
a comprehensive disaster management package in 2022, including a 14-week course for 
battalion commanders specifically tailored to disaster response. Training continues through 
live action drills and lessons learned from cyclones and other emergencies. However, these 
programmes are not yet mandated for the police and prison services, and interagency joint 
exercises remain rare. The Air Force of Zimbabwe operates a modest fleet, providing 
substantial air mobility for rapid deployment and resupply, though economic pressures and 
reliance on ageing equipment constrain operational readiness. Section 213 of the Constitution

--- Page 3 ---
clearly empowers the President to deploy the Defence Forces in support of civilian authorities 
during an emergency or disaster. 
Despite all these efforts, operationalisation remains hampered by underfunding, fuel shortages 
and delayed activation protocols. During Cyclone Idai, military helicopters arrived 72 hours 
after landfall due to unclear command channels, a gap that the new contingency plan attempts 
to address. However, without binding standard operating procedures, delays persist. Regional 
neighbours have progressed further. Mozambique’s Armed Forces pre-position troops, Malawi 
maintains a dedicated disaster response battalion, and South Africa’s National Defence Force 
operates a Joint Tactical Headquarters for disasters. Zimbabwe’s contingency plan is a positive 
step, but it lacks legislative backing and detailed interagency protocols. 
Despite these provisions, the law remains incomplete where it matters most: defining who does 
what, when, and under whose authority. The Zimbabwe Defence Forces Act (Chapter 11:02) 
mandates the ZDF to assist civil authorities in emergencies but does not define what constitutes 
an emergency or outline command relationships. The Civil Protection Act similarly omits the 
roles of the security sector. Consequently, integrated climate disaster training modules are 
absent from ordinary police or prison curricula, although military higher education has 
advanced in this area. These deficits translate into preventable loss of life and prolonged 
recovery periods. 
3.0 Legislative and Policy Framework 
The Civil Protection Act (Chapter 10:06), enacted in 1989 and last amended in 2001, remains 
Zimbabwe’s primary disaster management law. It centralises authority in the DCP but does not 
recognise climate change as a distinct hazard category nor mandate security sector integration. 
The government is now developing a more comprehensive Disaster Risk Management and 
Civil Protection Bill to replace the 1989 Act entirely. This was confirmed by the Ministry of 
Local Government in February 2026, and the new Bill aims to address modern threats such as 
droughts and enhance national capacity to prevent and reduce risks. Civil society, including 
ActionAid Zimbabwe, has called for timely finalisation of the Bill. A proposed Civil Protection 
Amendment Bill (2022) has remained pending, but the shift towards a full replacement Bill 
represents significant progress. 
The National Multi-Hazard Contingency Plan (2025/2026), endorsed by Cabinet, now provides 
an operational framework that formally integrates the ZDF. It represents a proactive shift, but 
it is not a legislative instrument. The National Climate Policy of 2017 acknowledges disaster 
risk reduction but defers to the Department of Civil Protection without detailing security sector 
functions. The Zimbabwe Defence Forces Act (Chapter 11:02) provides vague authority. While 
Section 213 of the Constitution already enables deployment, no subordinate legislation 
specifies activation thresholds, cost reimbursement or deactivation procedures. 
Overlapping mandates create confusion: during the 2024 drought, the DCP, Environmental 
Management Agency, ZDF and NGOs all conducted separate assessments without a unified 
command. Reforms must prioritise either amending the Civil Protection Act or passing the new 
Disaster Risk Management Bill to give legal force to the contingency plan’s provisions. 
Legislation should designate the security sector as a formal disaster response pillar with defined 
roles for the ZDF, ZRP and ZPCS. It should mandate annual joint simulations, establish a joint 
civil-military disaster coordination centre, and require climate-disaster modules in all security

--- Page 4 ---
sector training curricula, building on the ZDF’s existing programmes. Without these legislative 
changes, the 2025/2026 Contingency Plan remains a well-intentioned but unenforceable 
roadmap. 
4.0 Lessons for Zimbabwe from Regional Best Practices 
Mozambique, Malawi and South Africa have successfully integrated security sectors into 
disaster management through legislative mandates, dedicated units and binding protocols. 
• Mozambique formalised civil-military disaster cooperation following Cyclone Idai 
(2019) via Decree No. 78/2020, creating Provincial Disaster Management Committees 
with military voting powers. The Armed Forces (FADM) now pre-position engineering 
and medical units in cyclone-prone provinces, reducing response times from 72 to under 
12 hours. 
• Malawi established the Malawi Defence Force Disaster Response Battalion in 2018. 
This 800-person unit is trained in flood rescue, field hospital setup and aerial logistics. 
It operates under a joint command with the Department of Disaster Management Affairs 
through a signed memorandum of understanding. Between 2019 and 2023, this unit 
reduced flood mortality by 40 per cent. 
• South Africa institutionalised civil-military coordination through the Disaster 
Management Act (2002, amended 2015), mandating the SANDF to establish a Joint 
Tactical Headquarters for each declared disaster, with compulsory annual joint 
exercises. 
For Zimbabwe, these models demonstrate that a contingency plan alone is insufficient. Three 
pillars are required: (1) a legislative mandate clarifying roles and activation procedures; (2) 
dedicated units with climate-disaster specialisation; and (3) binding protocols (MoUs or SOPs) 
negotiated pre-disaster. Parliament should mandate the DCP, Ministry of Defence and Ministry 
of Local Government to negotiate a tripartite framework agreement within 12 months, building 
on the 2025/2026 Contingency Plan. 
5.0 Policy Options 
5.1. Specialised Climate-Disaster Training for All Security Forces 
Integrate climate change adaptation, disaster response and civil-military coordination modules 
into ZRP and ZPCS training curricula. Training for police and prisons should include 
hydrological forecasting, shelter management, contamination control, humanitarian principles 
and drone operation. Initial costs include curriculum development and train-the-trainer 
programmes. Benefits include faster, more professional responses and reduced civil-military 
friction. 
5.2. Dedicated Disaster Response Engineering and Air Mobility Units 
Establish a permanent ZDF Engineering Company (bridge construction, debris clearance, 
water purification) and augment existing air assets. While substantial capital and annual 
operating costs would be needed for specialised engineering equipment, fuel and maintenance, 
the benefits would be considerable: response times reduced from days to hours and access to 
remote districts such as Chimanimani, Binga and Mbire.

--- Page 5 ---
5.3. Advanced Technology Integration (Drones, GIS, Blockchain) 
Scale up the government’s drone pilot programme for high-risk area mapping and real-time 
damage assessment. Establish a National Disaster Geospatial Intelligence Unit within the DCP, 
staffed by ZDF geospatial analysts. Use blockchain-based aid tracking to prevent diversion and 
ensure transparency. Costs would include the acquisition of drones, GIS software and 
associated training. Benefits would include faster situational awareness, improved resource 
allocation and reduced corruption. 
5.4. Civil-Military Coordination Protocols (SOPs) 
Draft and mandate standard operating procedures for civil-military disaster response, covering: 
activation triggers (e.g., presidential declaration or DCP request), command and control 
(civilian-led with military liaison), resource reimbursement (national treasury to cover military 
costs), information sharing (joint situation rooms) and deactivation procedures. Development 
costs would be incurred, but the benefits include eliminated ambiguity, faster authorisation and 
accountability, directly addressing concerns over militarisation and centralised control. 
5.5. Enact the Disaster Risk Management and Civil Protection Bill 
Parliament should prioritise finalising and passing the new Disaster Risk Management and 
Civil Protection Bill, which replaces the outdated Civil Protection Act. The Bill should 
formally designate the security sector as a disaster response pillar, define specific ZDF, ZRP 
and ZPCS functions, mandate pre-positioning of assets during hazard seasons, and require 
annual joint simulations with civilian agencies. This would give legal force to the 2025/2026 
Contingency Plan and align with Section 213 of the Constitution. Costs would include 
parliamentary drafting and stakeholder validation. Benefits would include legal clarity, 
sustained political will and eligibility for international disaster response funding. 
5.6. Establish a Joint Civil-Military Disaster Coordination Centre 
Create a permanent, interagency coordination centre hosted by the DCP and co-staffed by the 
ZDF to maintain asset inventories, conduct risk mapping, facilitate pre-season planning and 
manage real-time information during emergencies. While initial setup costs would be required 
to cover communications, GIS systems and staffing, with additional annual running costs, the 
benefits include unified command, reduced duplication and institutional memory across 
disaster cycles, countering the current overcentralisation in Harare. 
5.7. Pre-Positioning and Contingency Funding 
Authorise the Ministry of Finance to allocate a dedicated annual contingency fund enabling 
pre-positioning of food, fuel, medical supplies and engineering stores in high-risk provinces 
(Manicaland, Masvingo, Matabeleland South). Benefits include self-sufficiency, reducing 
reliance on delayed NGO supplies, and faster first response within 6 to 12 hours of disaster 
onset. 
6.0 Recommendations 
Parliament should: 
• Enact the Disaster Risk Management and Civil Protection Bill to replace the Civil 
Protection Act (Chapter 10:06), giving legislative force to the 2025/2026 National

--- Page 6 ---
Multi-Hazard Contingency Plan, formally integrating the security sector and defining 
roles, activation criteria and command relationships, consistent with Section 213 of the 
Constitution. 
• Mandate specialised climate-disaster training for ZRP and ZPCS personnel, building 
on the ZDF’s existing MSc in Disaster Management and 14-week battalion commander 
course, and require annual joint simulations with civilian agencies. 
• Allocate resources for dedicated engineering units and ensure that the Air Force’s 
existing helicopters are properly fuelled and maintained for disaster response, 
acknowledging operational constraints from ageing equipment. 
• Adopt binding civil-military coordination protocols (SOPs) negotiated between the 
DCP, Ministry of Defence and Ministry of Local Government, addressing securitisation 
concerns by distinguishing enforcement roles from humanitarian support and clarifying 
civilian authority. 
• Establish a permanent Joint Civil-Military Disaster Coordination Centre to 
operationalise interagency planning, real-time response and advanced technology 
integration (drones, GIS, blockchain). 
• Create a contingency fund for pre-positioned disaster assets in climate-vulnerable 
provinces, managed jointly by the DCP and ZDF. 
• mandate the Zimbabwe Human Rights Commission to receive and investigate 
complaints of military overreach during disaster responses, with a 30-day reporting 
requirement 
7.0 Conclusion 
Climate-induced disasters are no longer exceptional events but recurring national security 
threats. Zimbabwe has taken important steps with the National Multi-Hazard Contingency Plan 
(2025/2026) and the development of the Disaster Risk Management and Civil Protection Bill. 
The ZDF possesses constitutional authority under Section 213, substantial air assets, and 
advanced training capacity. However, a plan without legislative backing, binding protocols and 
adequate funding remains fragile. Persistent challenges, resource shortages, centralised control 
and risks of militarisation must be addressed through the reforms outlined above. Short-term 
measures, including specialised training for police and prison services, binding SOPs, 
contingency funding and drone and GIS integration, combined with long-term legislative 
enactment, can transform the ZDF, ZRP and ZPCS into effective, accountable disaster response 
partners. Failure to act will perpetuate preventable suffering, economic loss and erosion of 
public trust. Parliament must lead the urgent process of integrating the security sector into 
climate adaptation, ensuring that those who defend the nation also protect it from the rising 
tides of climate change. 
(Disclaimer: The views expressed in this brief belong solely to the author and do not 
necessarily reflect the position of Parliament of Zimbabwe.)

--- Page 7 ---
2. Department of Disaster Management Affairs (DoDMA), Malawi. (2024). Evaluation 
of the MDF Disaster Response Battalion. Lilongwe: DoDMA. 
3. Instituto Nacional de Gestão de Calamidades (INGC), Mozambique. 
(2022). Post-Cyclone Idai Civil-Military Coordination Review. Maputo: INGC. 
4. Ministry of Local Government and Public Works, Zimbabwe. (2026). Disaster Risk 
Management and Civil Protection Bill: Policy Brief. Harare: MoLGPW 
5. Parliamentary Portfolio Committee on Defence and Home Affairs, Zimbabwe.

tracked_topics.full_content:
--- Page 1 ---
BLESSING CHIWANZA 1 
 
 
Policy Brief 1/2026: 
Zero-Rating vs VAT Exemption: Policy Choices for 
Industrial Competitiveness in Zimbabwe 
 
Executive Summary 
Zimbabwe’s industrialisation agenda, 
anchored in Vision 2030, is being 
constrained by persistently high production 
costs, low-capacity utilisation, and heavy 
reliance on imported inputs. The structure 
of the Value Added Tax (VAT) system 
particularly the distinction between zero-
rating and VAT exemption has emerged as a 
critical policy lever with direct implications 
for industrial performance. 
While both instruments aim to reduce the 
tax burden, their economic effects differ 
significantly. Zero-rating allows firms to 
reclaim input VAT, thereby lowering 
production costs and preserving 
competitiveness. VAT exemption, by 
contrast, prevents input tax recovery and 
embeds VAT into production costs. 
Current expansions in VAT exemptions risk 
increasing the cost of production at a time 
when Zimbabwe’s industrial capacity 
utilisation remains below optimal levels 
and firms continue to rely heavily on 
imported inputs. 
This approach may unintentionally weaken 
domestic manufacturing and slow industrial 
recovery. 
This brief recommends a strategic shift 
toward expanded zero-rating of productive 
inputs, supported by reforms to VAT refund 
administration, in order to reduce costs, 
support value addition, and enhance 
competitiveness.

--- Page 2 ---
BLESSING CHIWANZA 2 
 
Introduction 
Industrial Competitiveness and VAT 
Policy 
Zimbabwe’s industrial sector continues to 
operate below potential, constrained by 
high input costs, foreign currency 
shortages, and competition from imports. 
Manufacturing firms rely significantly on 
imported raw materials, making them 
highly sensitive to tax policy on imports. 
VAT, governed by the Value Added Tax Act 
[Chapter 23:12], is levied on goods and 
services as well as imports. While designed 
to be neutral, its impact depends on how 
goods are classified within the system. 
VAT policy is therefore not merely a 
revenue instrument it directly influences 
production costs, pricing structures, and 
investment decisions. Poorly designed VAT 
measures can raise costs and discourage 
local production, while well-designed 
measures can support industrial growth and 
competitiveness. 
Zero-Rating vs VAT Exemption: The 
Policy Distinction 
The VAT Act provides two mechanisms for 
tax relief: 
Section 10 (Zero-Rating): Supplies are 
taxed at 0%, allowing firms to reclaim input 
VAT. 
Section 11 (Exemption): Supplies are not 
taxed, but firms cannot recover input VAT. 
Zero-rating preserves VAT neutrality by 
ensuring that taxation does not increase 
production costs along the value chain. VAT 
exemption, however, results in embedded 
tax costs, effectively increasing the cost of 
production. 
Failure to maintain VAT neutrality raises 
production costs, distorts pricing, and 
weakens competitiveness, particularly in 
import-dependent manufacturing sectors. 
Economic Implications for Zimbabwean 
Industry 
For Zimbabwean manufacturers, the 
distinction between zero-rating and VAT 
exemption has direct implications for 
production costs and competitiveness. 
Under a zero-rating regime, firms are able 
to recover VAT paid on inputs, thereby 
lowering their cost base and improving 
their pricing competitiveness in both 
domestic and export markets. In contrast, 
VAT exemption prevents the recovery of 
input tax, effectively converting VAT into a 
cost of production, which increases 
operating expenses, compresses margins, 
and raises final prices. Evidence from the 
International Growth Centre indicates that 
VAT exemptions raise the effective tax 
burden on firms by embedding

--- Page 3 ---
BLESSING CHIWANZA 3 
 
unrecoverable input VAT, particularly in 
manufacturing sectors, while Warwick et al. 
(2022) show that such regimes distort 
supply chains and reduce productivity. In 
Zimbabwe, these effects are intensified by 
high dependence on imported raw 
materials, persistent foreign currency 
constraints, and limited domestic 
production of intermediate goods. As a 
result, VAT exemption policies risk 
increasing production costs at a time when 
industrial recovery depends on improving 
efficiency, reducing input costs, and 
strengthening competitiveness. 
Administrative Efficiency and 
Implementation Constraints 
Although VAT exemption is often perceived 
as administratively simpler, it introduces 
classification ambiguities and increases 
opportunities for tax avoidance, particularly 
where distinctions between exempt and 
taxable goods are unclear. Zero-rating is 
more consistent with efficient VAT design 
but depends on a well-functioning refund 
system to ensure that firms can recover 
input VAT in a timely manner. 
In Zimbabwe, delays in VAT refunds 
continue to impose significant liquidity 
constraints on businesses, particularly in 
manufacturing, effectively tying up 
working capital and increasing the cost of 
financing operations. Addressing this 
challenge requires targeted administrative 
reforms within the Zimbabwe Revenue 
Authority, including the digitisation of 
refund processes, enforcement of time-
bound refund periods, and strengthening of 
institutional capacity. Improving refund 
efficiency is therefore critical to ensuring 
that zero-rating delivers its intended 
benefits and supports industrial activity. 
Comparative Insights from Peer 
Economies 
Experiences from peer economies in Africa 
demonstrate the limitations of VAT 
exemptions as a tool for supporting 
industrial development. In South Africa, the 
Davis Tax Committee found that 
exemptions often resulted in inefficiencies 
and poor targeting, reducing their 
effectiveness. Studies in Ghana and 
Ethiopia similarly show that VAT 
exemptions increase production costs, 
encourage informality, and weaken tax 
compliance. In contrast, countries that have 
prioritised VAT neutrality through zero-
rating have achieved better outcomes in 
terms of industrial competitiveness, supply 
chain efficiency, and formal sector 
participation. Evidence from Warwick et al. 
(2022) further indicates that replacing VAT 
exemptions with more neutral policy 
instruments improves both efficiency and 
equity outcomes. These findings highlight

--- Page 4 ---
BLESSING CHIWANZA 4 
 
that VAT policy design plays a critical role 
in shaping industrial performance and 
should be aligned with broader economic 
development objectives. 
Policy Options 
Option A: Maintain the Current VAT 
Structure 
Retain the existing mix of zero-rating and 
VAT exemptions. This provides short-term 
relief but continues to raise production 
costs and weaken industrial 
competitiveness. 
Option B: Replace VAT Relief with 
Targeted Subsidies 
Use direct subsidies or transfers instead of 
VAT adjustments. Allows precise targeting 
but is fiscally demanding and 
administratively complex to implement at 
scale. 
Option B: Expand Zero-Rating for 
Strategic Inputs (Preferred Option) 
Extend zero-rating to cover all strategic raw 
materials and intermediate goods used in 
key industrial and agricultural value chains. 
This has an impact of reducing production 
costs, enhances competitiveness, and 
supports value addition, but requires 
improved VAT refund administration. 
 
Recommendations 
1. Parliament should amend the Value 
Added Tax Act [Chapter 23:12] to expand 
the zero-rating schedule to include all 
strategic raw materials and intermediate 
inputs in manufacturing and agriculture. 
2. The Ministry of Finance, Economic 
Development and Investment Promotion 
should conduct a comprehensive review of 
VAT exemptions and implement a phased 
transition toward zero-rating for productive 
inputs. 
3. The Zimbabwe Revenue Authority 
should modernise VAT refund systems 
through digitalisation and enforce statutory 
timeframes for refunds to improve business 
liquidity. 
4. The Ministry of Industry and Commerce 
should integrate VAT policy into the 
National Industrial Development Policy by 
identifying priority sectors requiring zero-
rated inputs. 
5. The Ministry of Finance, in collaboration 
with ZIMSTAT, should establish a 
monitoring framework to assess the impact 
of VAT policy on industrial performance, 
investment, and import substitution.

--- Page 5 ---
BLESSING CHIWANZA 5 
 
Conclusion 
The distinction between zero-rating and 
VAT exemption represents a critical policy 
choice with direct implications for 
Zimbabwe’s industrial competitiveness. 
VAT exemption effectively increases 
production costs by embedding input taxes, 
while zero-rating supports efficiency and 
competitiveness by preserving VAT 
neutrality. 
At a time when Zimbabwe’s industrial 
sector requires cost reduction and 
productivity gains, expanding VAT 
exemptions risks reinforcing structural 
constraints. A strategic shift toward zero-
rating, supported by administrative 
reforms, offers a clear pathway to support 
industrial recovery and long-term economic 
growth. 
Aligning VAT policy with national 
development objectives is therefore 
essential to advancing Zimbabwe’s Vision 
2030 and strengthening the foundations of 
domestic production. 
 
 
 
 
 
References 
1. Government of Zimbabwe (n.d.) Value 
Added Tax Act [Chapter 23:12]. 
Harare: Government of Zimbabwe. 
2. International Growth Centre (2018) 
VAT and Firms in Developing 
Countries. London: International 
Growth Centre. 
3. Warwick, R., Harris, T., Phillips, D. and 
Goldman, M. (2022) ‘The redistributive 
power of VAT exemptions versus cash 
transfers’, World Development, 151.

--- Page 1 ---
Page1 
 
Policy Brief: 
The Future of Burial Space in Zimbabwe – A Growing Land Crisis in 
Urban Areas 
 
 
 
 
Executive Summary 
The increasing number of annual deaths in Zimbabwe is leading to a growing demand for burial spaces, 
putting pressure on available land. Given that many Zimbabweans oppose cremation and the reuse of 
old graves due to cultural and spiritual beliefs, cemeteries are rapidly consuming land that could 
otherwise be used for agriculture and development in urban areas. This policy brief projects the long-
term implications of burial practices on land availability and explores sustainable solutions to balance 
cultural traditions with land conservation. 
 
Introduction 
 As Zimbabwe's population grows and 
urbanization expands, the demand for burial 
space is becoming an unsustainable land use 
issue. Traditional cemeteries are rapidly 
expanding, encroaching on agricultural land 
and limiting future development opportunities. 
This increasing demand for burial sites poses a 
threat to sustainable development and food 
security. Additionally, due to cultural beliefs, 
many Zimbabweans reject cremation and 
cemetery reuse, further exacerbating the need 
for new burial spaces. 
 
Target Audience 
• Parliamentarians and policymakers 
• Urban and rural planners 
• Traditional and religious leaders 
 
Objective of the Policy Brief 
To project the impact of burial space 
consumption in Zimbabwe. 
 
Cultural and Religious Beliefs on Burial 
Practices 
Cultural and religious traditions in Zimbabwe 
strongly influence burial practices. Cremation 
is widely rejected due to beliefs in ancestral 
spirits and deep respect for the deceased. Many 
fear that disturbing human remains may bring 
misfortune, making exhumation or grave reuse 
unacceptable. Additionally, communities 
oppose repurposing cemetery land for 
agriculture or development, as gravesites hold 
profound spiritual significance. These beliefs 
make it challenging to introduce alternative 
burial methods despite growing land shortages. 
Evidence Analysis

--- Page 2 ---
Page2 
Annual Death Registrations and Projected 
Burial Space Needs 
According to the Zimbabwe National Statistics 
Agency (ZIMSTAT), the number of deaths 
registered annually has risen due to factors such 
as disease outbreaks, road accidents, and 
natural causes. The following data from 2020 -
2024 shows the number of deaths per year: 
• 2020: 126,360 deaths 
• 2021: 138,736 deaths 
• 2022: 124,999 deaths 
• 2023: 124,412 deaths 
• 2024: 124,718 deaths 
Source: https://database.earth/population/zimbabwe/deaths 
 
Considering the five-year average of 
127,845 deaths per year, with each grave 
requiring 3 square meters, the annual land 
consumption for burials amounts to 
383,535 square meters. This growing 
demand for burial space raises concerns 
about sustainable land use, particularly as 
urban areas expand and available land 
becomes increasingly scarce. As the 
population continues to grow, the burial 
rate is expected to rise, placing pressure on 
land resources especially in urban areas. 
The following Figure 1 presents a 
projection of deaths from 2025 to 2100, 
highlighting the increasing need for burial 
space planning and alternative solutions. 
Figure 1: Future Population Deaths In 
Zimbabwe (2025-2100). 
 
 
 
Source: https://dtabase.earth/population/zimbabwe/deaths 
 
As the burial rate is projected to rise annually to 
352,325 burials, the demand for burial land will 
increase correspondingly. 
 
 With an initial estimate of 125,303 burials 
annually, and each individual requiring 3 
square meters of land, the total burial space 
consumed per year amounts to 375,909 square 
meters. At this higher rate, the total land 
required per year would surge to 1,056,975 
square meters. This growing need for burial 
space highlights the pressing concern of land 
allocation and long-term planning for 
cemeteries, particularly as Zimbabwe faces an 
ever-expanding population and the inevitability 
of mortality. 
 
Policy Options and Recommendations 
1. Introduce vertical burial structures to minimize land use. 
2. Provide incentives for voluntary cremation while respecting cultural sensitivities. 
3. Educate communities on sustainable burial practices. 
Conclusion 
Zimbabwe faces a burial space crisis due to population growth, urbanization, and cultural resistance to 
alternative burial methods. As cemeteries consume increasing amounts of agricultural land, 
policymakers must act now to ensure culturally appropriate and sustainable burial solutions. Sustainable 
alternatives, such as cremation and vertical cemeteries, must be explored. 
 
References 
• Zimbabwe National Statistics Agency (ZIMSTAT) Reports, 2020–2023 
• Moyo, T. (2022). "Urban Cemetery Challenges in Zimbabwe: A Case Study of Harare." 
• Chikowore, P. & Dube, R. (2021). "Cultural Perspectives on Cremation and Burial Practices 
in Zimbabwe." 
• Government of Zimbabwe, Ministry of Local Government and Public Works Policy Reports 
(2023). 
• https://database.earth/population/zimbabwe/deaths

--- Page 1 ---
PARLIAMENT OF ZIMBABWE 
Thursday, 25th July, 2024 
The National Assembly met at a Quarter-past Two o’clock p.m. 
PRAYERS 
(THE HON. DEPUTY SPEAKER in the Chair) 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE, ECONOMIC 
DEVELOPMENT AND INVESTMENT PROMOTION (HON. 
PROF. NCUBE): I move that leave be granted to present 2024 Mid-
Year Budget and Economic Review Statement. The Review Statement… 
THE HON. DEPUTY SPEAKER: Hon. Minister, please may 
you hold on for a moment. 
HON. M. C. SIBANDA: Thank you Madam Speaker. I want to 
congratulate the team of seven national athletes for representing us in the 
2024 Athletics in Paris. However, the number in composition of the 
officials is of public and national concern, given that the Ministry and 
Government is committed in other areas such as the National Sports 
Stadium and our roads from Bulawayo to Victoria Falls. I thank you.

--- Page 2 ---
THE HON. DEPUTY SPEAKER: Thank you Hon. Sibanda. I 
advise you to bring a motion to this House in that regard. Thank you. 
*HON. HAMAUSWA: Thank you Madam Speaker and good 
afternoon. I was just looking at the Constitution of Zimbabwe and other 
Conventions, which preserve political rights and the right to assemble, 
particularly as we are looking forward to hosting the SADC Summit and 
visitors who will be coming. The continued incarceration of the 
Zimbabwean citizens, which is covered by the Constitution, allows 
people freedom of assemble. If there are tangible reasons of why people 
are being incarcerated, this should be brought even to this august House. 
Yesterday, ZINASU students … 
 *HON. TAFANANA ZHOU: On a point of order, Madam 
Speaker Ma’am, the Hon. Member is talking about issues that are before 
the courts. We do not talk about what is happening in the courts in this 
august House. 
 *THE HON. DEPUTY SPEAKER: Thank you Hon. Zhou, I 
will allow the Hon. Member to finish.

--- Page 3 ---
*HON. HAMAUSWA: Thank you Madam Speaker Ma’am. The 
issue I am talking about is not before the courts, like every Harare MP is 
not allowed to have feedback meetings. The issue that I was talking 
about is an issue which pertains to what happened yesterday where 
ZINASU students were having a capacity building meeting and they 
were arrested. The issue of the continued incarceration, arresting of 
people every day does not paint a good picture. We will be having 
ambassadors from the SADC region. This is painting the country in bad 
light – [HON. MEMBERS: Inaudible interjections.]- 
 Hon. Togarepi and Hon. Z. Ziyambi having stood up. 
 THE HON. DEPUTY SPEAKER: Hon. Togarepi, please may 
you take your seat. Hon. Minister, what do you want to say? 
 THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE, LEGAL AND 
PARLIAMENTARY AFFAIRS (HON. Z. ZIYAMBI): Madam 
Speaker, this is not a forum for Hon. Members to abuse and come with 
falsehoods. We do not have a crisis, the police are carrying out their 
duty. If he has any issues with the conduct of the police, he knows what

--- Page 4 ---
he is supposed to do. He should not abuse the audience that he has here 
in the House to speak about issues of the police. 
 *THE HON. DEPUTY SPEAKER: Let me respond to Hon. 
Hamauswa. I have heard you but I request that since it is a specific 
request, please put it in writing so we can ask the responsible Minister to 
bring the response. 
 HON. MANGONDO: I rise on a point of national interest. I 
want to speak on an issue that weighs heavily on my heart and the 
conscience of our nation. Madam Speaker Ma’am, I feel compelled to 
address the plight of the Palestinian people and our deep-rooted

tracked_topics.full_content:
--- Page 1 ---
1 
 
 
 
BILLS DIGEST 2023 
 
NAME PRISONS AND CORRECTIONAL SERVICES BILL, 
HB NUMBER H.B.6, 2022 
MINISTRY JUSTICE, LEGAL AND PARLIAMENTARY AFFAIRS 
DATE FEBRUARY 2023 
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 
 
1.0 INTRODUCTION 
The Prison and Correctional Services Bill was gazetted on 07th October 2022. The Bill, among 
others things seeks to repeal the Prisons Act and according to its memorandum, provides for 
the following: 
• the establishment, functions, and administration of the Prisons and Correctional 
Service; 
• the establishment of the Prisons and Correctional Service Commission; 
• the establishment of prisons and correctional facilities; 
• the functions, rights, obligations, and discipline of prison officers; 
• the safe custody of all offenders under humane conditions that respect human 
dignity; 
• the discipline of offenders; 
• the obligations and rights of sentenced offenders; 
• the obligations and rights of unsentenced offenders; 
• the establishment of a parole system; 
• the mechanism to deal with complaints of abuse of offenders; 
• the judicial and civilian oversight of the operations of the Service; and 
• the penalties for offences; and 
• the repeal of the Prisons Act and the substitution of an Act entitled the Prisons and 
Correctional Service Act. 
2.0 BACKGROUND 
The Prisons Act [Chapter 7:11] was enacted into law on 23 April 1956, and was last amended 
in 20041. This piece of legislation, dating back to the mid-1950s is clearly now inadequate and 
out of sync with the international norms and standards relating to prison administration. The 
Prisons and Correctional Service is a department under the Ministry of Justice, Legal and 
 
1 The Act was amended in the Criminal Law (Codification and Reform) Act [Chapter 9:23] (No. 23/2004).

--- Page 2 ---
2 
 
Parliamentary Affairs and is also a security service under section 207 (d) of the Constitution. 
Section 227 of the Constitution establish the Prisons and Correctional Service whose 
responsibility is: 
i. Protection of society from criminals through the incarceration and rehabilitation of 
convicted persons and others who are lawfully required to be detained, and their 
reintegration into society; and 
ii. The administration of prisons and correctional facilities. 
Section 227(2) of the Constitution lays down the non-partisan nature of the Service, its national 
character and other attributes. Section 230 of the Constitution establishes the Prisons and 
Correctional Service Commission, which is tasked with the employment and regulation of 
members of the Service. 
However, the legal framework governing its functions and operations remained unaddressed. 
The broadening of the scope of the Zimbabwe Prisons and Correctional Services mandate 
necessitated the review of the current Act to ensure that the legislation is in sync with the 
Constitution. The thrust of modern-day Prisons and Correctional Services is now more on 
restorative justice as opposed to punishment of offenders. 
Therefore, the Bill seeks to effect the provisions of the Constitution establishing a Correctional 
Service. It will determine how the Service is run, how officers join the Service, their 
disciplinary matters and regulation by the Service and the role of the Prison and Correctional 
Service Commission. The Bill seeks to modernize the prison legislation to ensure that it meets 
international norms and standards of prison administration and treatment of prisoners. It seeks 
to ensure that the prison system caters for the needs of vulnerable groups such as pregnant 
women, juvenile offenders, persons with disabilities, and other special categories that have 
special needs. 
 
3.0 SUMMARY AND ANALYSIS OF CLAUSES 
Clauses 1 and 2 provide for the short title of the Bill and the definition of terms used in the 
Bill. 
Clauses 3 provides for the establishment of the Zimbabwe Prisons and Correctional Service, 
comprising of the Commissioner-General, one or more Deputy Commissioner-Generals and 
correctional officers of various ranks. 
 Clause 4 provides for the principles of the service. 
Comment: The Bill explicitly refers to principles to guide the Service, which the current Act 
does not have. The principles include the factors to be taken into account in the administration 
of a prison sentence shall, relevant policies, conditions of service that positively impact on 
officers, among other matters. 
Clause 5 provides for the functions of the service.

--- Page 3 ---
3 
 
Comment: The current Act is silent on some of the issues provided for under this clause, which 
are taken from the human rights ethos of the Constitution, as well as international norms and 
best practice in respect of persons under arrest, custody and detention. By making reference 
to issues of human rights, healthcare and rehabilitation, the provisions differentiate the former 
Prison Service from a Correctional Service as envisaged under the Constitution. 
Clause 8 provides for the appointment and retirement of the Commissioner-General 
Comment: Section 7 of the Prisons Act provides that the Commissioner-General is appointed 
for a four-year renewable term. The Bill provides that the Commissioner-General can only be 
appointed for a term of 5 years. However, the Bill is silent on whether the term is renewable 
or not. 
Clauses 16 to 23 provide for the Prison and Correctional Service Commission, its functions 
and the term of office for a member of the Commission, which shall be a period five years 
renewable only once. The clauses provide for the staff, procedure and reports of the 
Commission. It provides that the Service shall report annually to the Minister. 
Clauses 24 to 32 and it provides for the establishment, administration and control of Prisons 
and Correctional facilities. 
Clause 25 provides that temporary prisons and correction facilities can be established. 
Clauses 26 and 27 provide for the creation of correctional community centres, which may either 
be permanent or temporary, for the purpose of easing the transition of the inmate from life in 
incarceration to community life. 
Clause 28 provides for the establishment of open correctional facilities. 
Clause 30 provides for the confinement of male and female inmates separately. 
Clause 31 provides for the appointment of officers-in-charge of prison and correctional 
facilities and their functions. 
Clause 32 provides for the inspection of prisons and correctional facilities. 
Clauses 33 to 42 provide for the functions of correctional officers. 
Clauses 33 and 34 provide for the general responsibilities and functions of correctional officers. 
Clauses 35, 36 and 37 provide for things against which correctional officers should not do. 
Clauses 38, 39, gives correctional officers certain powers in the administration of prisons and 
correctional facilities. 
Clause 40 provides that no correctional officer shall, except in the case of sickness or 
emergency, enter a prison or correctional cell or ward at night unless accompanied by another 
correctional officer. 
Clauses 41 and 42 provide for immunity for acts done legally and on reasonable grounds 
respectively by any the Commissioner-General or any correctional officer.

--- Page 4 ---
4 
 
Clauses 43 to 69 provide for the disciplinary procedure that may be pursued against 
correctional officers for acts of indiscipline perpetrated. 
Clause 70 and 71 provide for the admission of inmates into custodial imprisonment and for 
conditions of admission to prison of a female inmate with an infant and that with pregnancy. It 
provides that the State shall provide food for infants of female inmates for 59 months, at which 
point the infant may be handed over to a relative or friend of the mother. The provision also 
enjoins the Service to provide ante-natal and post-natal facilities, within the limit of resources 
available to the State. 
Comment: It is important to note that the Bill incorporates the best interests of the child 
principle. 
Clause 72 allows for the maintenance of unconvicted inmates from private sources apart from 
receiving normal prison food, clothing and bedding. 
Clause 73 provides for the disposal of inmates’ personal effects. 
Clause 74 provides that moneys on inmate at the time of being admitted to prison may be 
appropriated for the payment of fine. 
Clause 75 provides for the commencement, termination and computation of sentence of 
imprisonment imposed by any court unless the sentence is suspended in terms of any law or 
the convicted person is released on bail granted in terms of any law. 
Clause 76 provides for the separation, security classification and re-classification of inmates 
into one or more of the stipulated groups. 
Clause 77 gives the officer-in-charge of a given prison responsibility to ensure lawful custody 
of an imprisoned inmate. 
Clause 78 requires that inmates in imprisonment be under the care, custody and supervision of 
correctional officers of the same sex with them. 
Clause 79 provides for the custody of inmates committed for remand. 
Clause 80 provides for custody of juvenile offenders. It provides that juvenile offenders shall 
not be detained in a correctional facility unless the court so orders. 
Comment: This is in line with amendments carried in the Child Justice Bill, which seeks to 
avoid the incarceration of juvenile offenders. 
Clause 81 provides for the escort of inmates by police where on the removal of any inmate 
from any prison or correctional facility, the number of correctional officers is insufficient to 
provide an escort for such inmate. 
Clause 82 provides that where an inmate is required to attend a court for the purposes of 
testifying at any of its proceedings the court may issue an order directed to the officer-in-charge 
of the prison or correctional facility where that inmate is detained requiring him or her to 
produce the inmate at the time and place specified in the order, and the officer-in-charge shall 
comply with such order.

--- Page 5 ---
5 
 
Clause 83 requires that an inmate, before commencement of, and during his or her trial, be 
afforded adequate facilities in the prison or correctional facility or other place of detention for 
the preparation and presentation of his or her defence. 
Clause 84 provides for the questioning of an inmate by a member of the police, which may be 
done in the sight and hearing of a correctional officer. This is done with the approval of the 
officer-in-charge of a prison or correctional facility and on production of an order in writing 
from a police officer of or above such rank as may be prescribed. 
Clause 85 provides for the transfer of an inmate from one correctional facility to another. 
Clause 86 provides for the maximum period of extended imprisonment. 
Clause 87 requires that inmates be informed of the provisions of the Act and applicable rules, 
orders and directives. 
Clause 88 requires the Commissioner-General to provide inmates with the opportunity to 
contribute to decisions of the Service that affect their welfare. 
Clauses 89 and 90 provide for the promotion and maintenance of a relationship between the 
inmate, family and community and facilitation of successful reintegration of the inmate into 
the society through visitations, receiving of letters, procurement of necessities and other 
privileges. 
Clauses 91 to 101 provide for the health care services for inmates and hygiene. The Bill will 
provide for extensive health care services for inmates in compliance with section 48 as read 
with section 50 of the Constitution on the rights of detained persons. It will extend inmates’ 
right to consult with a medical practitioner of their choice at their own expense. 
Comment: The clause incorporates health rights issues, which are not carried in the principal 
Act. Access to health services and the duty to take into account medical advice is taken aboard. 
Clauses 102 to 112 provide for the upholding of a safe environment within the correctional 
facility by stipulating procedures for the search, seizure, arrest and dealing with prohibited 
articles. 
Clauses 113 to 121 provides for disciplinary issues relating to inmates within the prison and 
correctional service. It deals with the stipulated procedure for Part I Correctional Offences and 
Part II Correctional Offences outlined the Third Schedule. 
Clauses 122-127 provides for the work and rehabilitation activities for inmates. It distinguishes 
between work of convicted inmates and work of unconvicted inmates, agreements for 
employment and training of inmates and gratuities for inmates. Part XI of the Bill provides for 
the rehabilitative aspects of the Service. 
Comment: This is in keeping with the thrust which incorporates rehabilitation of offenders. 
Clauses 129 and 130 
Comment: The Bill does not have clauses 129 and 130

--- Page 6 ---
6 
 
Clauses 130 provides for the maintenance of an admission register. 
Clause 131 provides for the re-arrest of inmates released erroneously. 
Clause 132 provides for imprisonment on default of payment of a fine. 
Clause 133 provides for periodic imprisonment. 
Clause 134 provides for confinement and restraint of inmate. 
Clauses 135 and 135 provide for inmates under sentence of death and persons who may have 
access to them 
Clause 137 provides for attendance at execution. 
Clause 138 provides for commutation of death sentence to sentence of imprisonment. 
Clauses 139 to 161 provide for the establishment the State Parole Board whose functions are 
to recommend to the Minister the release of inmates and authorise the release of inmates. The 
clauses set out the principles that guide the State Parole Board in fulfilling its functions. The 
clauses provide for conditions for the release of inmates. The Bill also seeks to broaden the 
scope of the parole system by providing eligibility for parole to every prisoner regardless of 
the nature of the sentences they are serving. 
Comment: This will make prisoner pardons and paroles more transparent. 
Clauses 162 to 168 provide for visiting justices and their functions, appointment of official 
visitors and their functions, and for official visitors to record visits in a prescribed book, visits 
by Ministers of Religion, probation officers and representatives of inmates’ aid societies. 
Clause 169 provides for appointment of a Correctional Board of Visitors whose role shall be 
to act as an oversight and advisory committee of citizens to represent the interests of people in 
prison and correctional facilities and shall meet at least four times a year. 
Clause 170 provides for the need to deliver a list of unconvicted inmates to the High Court on 
a quarterly basis giving details of when they were admitted to prison. This will ensure that 
unconvicted prisoners are tried within a reasonable period of time as a way of decongesting 
prisons and avoiding lengthy remands. 
Clause 171 provides for reporting on long term inmates every four years 
Clause 172 and 173 provides for the granting of an inmate permission to be temporarily absent 
from prison or correctional facility for personal, family or other reasons and home leave. 
Permission for absence is given under escort while home leave is granted to an inmate 
unescorted. 
Clause 174 provides for limitations on temporary absence and home leave. These privileges 
can only be authorised within Zimbabwe. 
Clause 175 provides that the police may provide assistance to the prisons and correctional 
service on request by the Commissioner-General of the Prisons and Correctional Service in an 
emergency situation.

--- Page 7 ---
7 
 
Clauses 176 and 177 relate to rewards for apprehension of escaped inmates, rewards or 
gratuities for correctional officers who, in the course of duty, have suffered bodily injuries, 
performed special acts of bravery or rendered any other special or meritorious service. 
Clauses 178 and 179 provide for the detention of inmates sentenced abroad and the transfer of 
inmates to other countries respectively. 
Clause 180 provides that service clubs and canteens shall be exempt from paying certain taxes, 
duties and fees. 
Clause 181 gives the Minister power to appoint a committee of inquiry whenever he or she 
considers it necessary, which committee will report to him or her on any matter relating to 
either or both the administration of any prison or correctional facility or the conditions of 
service of correctional officers; or any matter connected therewith. 
Clause 182 provides that the Minister may give policy directions of a general nature in the 
public interest. 
Clause 183 allows the Minster to make regulations relation to the Prisons and Correctional 
Service. 
Clauses 184, 185 and 186 relate to certain offences that may be committed and that notices in 
respect of offences that may be committed in prisons and correctional service facilities and the 
penalties attaching to such offences be displayed. 
4.0 CONCLUSION 
The Bill makes commendable effort in legislating for the incarceration and rehabilitation of 
offenders, in line with international standards and trends. It provides a framework to facilitate 
the execution of the institution’s mission to ‘protect society from criminal elements through 
the incarceration and rehabilitation of offenders for their successful reintegration into society 
while exercising reasonable, safe, secure and humane control’.

TITLE 2 
 
Chapter 2:09 To Top Page 
 
PUBLIC BODIES PRIVATE BILL PROCEDURE ACT 
Acts 35/1885, 24/1962 (s. 2); R.G.N. 387/1971. 
ARRANGEMENT OF SECTIONS 
Section 
 1. Short title. 
 2. Interpretation. 
 3. Public meeting to be convened to consider introducing or opposing 
private Bills. 
 4. Public meeting, how convened and publication of notice required. 
 5. Meeting assembled elects chairman, but may adjourn. 
 6. Resolution carried by two-thirds of meeting. 
 7. Voting by show of hands or upon demand by signature of list. 
 8. Lists to lie open for signature by rate payers. 
 9. Scrutiny of lists by chairman; result to be published at expense of 
public body. 
 10. Costs of introducing or opposing private Bill. 
AN ACT to authorize certain public bodies to introduce into and promote or to 
oppose in Parliament certain private Bills, and to legalize expenses incurred by such 
bodies in respect of the introduction and promotion of or the opposition to such 
private Bills. 
[Date of commencement: 10th June, 1891.] 
1 Short title 
This Act may be cited as the Public Bodies Private Bill Procedure Act [Chapter 2:09]. 
2 Interpretation 
In this Act— 
“local newspaper", in relation to any public body, means any newspaper circulating in 
the neighbourhood wherein all or most of the persons reside who are liable to pay 
rates to a public body; 
“public body" means any public body empowered to levy rates; 
“public meeting” means a public meeting summoned or convened in terms of section 
three; 
“ratepayer” means any person liable to the payment of rates to or qualified to vote in 
the election of members of a public body. 
3 Public meeting to be convened to consider introducing or opposing private 
Bills 
When any public body deems it expedient and necessary to introduce into Parliament 
and there promote any private Bill in furtherance of, or to oppose in Parliament any 
private Bill inconsistent or conflicting with, the interests of the general body of 
ratepayers upon whom such public body is by law empowered to levy rates, it shall 
be lawful for such public body to convene a public meeting of such ratepayers in 
accordance with this Act, for the purpose of laying before such meeting resolutions in 
favour of the introduction and promotion of or in favour of opposition to such private 
Bill, as the case may be. 
4 Public meeting, how convened and publication of notice required 
Every public meeting shall be convened to assemble at some convenient time and 
place and upon a day to be stated in a notice of such meeting, and the notice shall be 
published not less than four times in any one or more local newspapers or, in default 
of any local newspaper, in every issue of the Gazette during a period of not less than 
two weeks before the stated day, and shall refer to this Act and shall contain as nearly 
as may be the words of the resolution or resolutions to be proposed for the 
TITLE 2

--- Page 2 ---
consideration of the public meeting, and also a clear general statement of the object 
and purpose of the public meeting. 
5 Meeting assembled elects chairman, but may adjourn 
At the time and place and on the day specified in the notice the public meeting shall 
assemble, and a chairman shall be forthwith elected by a vote of the majority of 
ratepayers present and voting at such meeting by show of hands, but thereafter the 
said meeting may, by resolution of the majority of ratepayers present and voting, be 
adjourned for any period not longer than one week to re-assemble at such time and 
place and on such day as by such resolution shall be determined. 
6 Resolution carried by two-thirds of meeting 
At any public meeting, or at any adjourned meeting thereof, as the case may be, the 
resolution or resolutions published in the notice of the meeting shall be submitted to 
the ratepayers thereat assembled, and if, by a vote of a majority of two-thirds of the 
ratepayers then present and voting, any such resolution to introduce and promote or to 
oppose any private Bill is carried, the public body which has convened the meeting 
shall be deemed and taken for all legal intents and purposes to be authorized to 
introduce and promote or to oppose such private Bill. 
7 Voting by show of hands or upon demand by signature of list 
The voting at any public meeting on the resolutions published in the notice of such 
meeting shall in the first place be by show of hands to be declared by the chairman, 
and the declaration of the chairman shall be final and conclusive, unless not less than 
twenty ratepayers present demand that the voting shall be by signature, and whenever 
any such demand is made the voting on the resolution in question shall be determined 
by signatures to be affixed by each ratepayer signing his name in full upon one of 
certain lists to be ready for the purpose at the meeting, and such lists shall be two in 
number for each resolution, and the signatures to the one list shall be in affirmation 
and to the other in negation of the resolution in question. 
8 Lists to lie open for signature by rate payers 
The lists referred to in section seven shall, at a place or places to be notified from the 
chair at such meeting, lie open on a day to be named by the chairman, being not less 
than seven and not more than fourteen days from the date of meeting, and between 
the hours of ten o’clock in the morning and four o’clock in the afternoon on such day, 
and may be signed by any ratepayer during the said period and hours. 
9 Scrutiny of lists by chairman; result to be published at expense of public body 
Every list referred to in section seven shall, after the termination of the period it lies 
open, be scrutinized by the chairman elected by the meeting, together with such 
assistants as the public body concerned may appoint, and the result of the voting shall 
be declared by the chairman by advertisement to be published at least twice in one or 
more local newspapers, or in the Gazette, at the expense of the ordinary revenue of 
the public body. 
10 Costs of introducing or opposing private Bill 
When any resolution is carried in favour of the introduction and promotion of, or in 
favour of opposition to, any private Bill in terms of this Act, all necessary costs, 
charges and expenses incurred by the public body concerned in and about the 
convening of the meeting and the introduction and promotion of or opposition to the 
private Bill, shall be payable out of the ordinary revenue derived by such public body 
from rates levied on the ratepayers, notwithstanding anything to the contrary 
contained in any enactment.

tracked_topics.full_content:
--- Page 1 ---
STATUTORY PROVISIONS ON REFERENDUMS FOR CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS IN ZIMBABWE 
 
FACT SHEET 
[By Agnes Zamila] 
The procedure for amending the Constitution of Zimbabwe is governed by section 328 of the Constitution of 
Zimbabwe (2013), the Referendums Act (Chapter 2:10) and the Electoral Act (Chapter 2:13). According to 
the constitution [Section 328(6), (7) & (8)] a referendum is mandatory where amendments relate to the 
declaration of rights (Chapter 4), agricultural land (Chapter 16), term limits of the President (Section 328), 
and presidential tenure and extension of office (Section 328) [see Mapungu vs Minister of Justice, Legal & 
Parliamentary Affairs]. 
 
Governing Legislation and Referendum Rules 
Constitution of Zimbabwe (2013) 
Section 328 
 
Governs when a referendum is mandatory — relating 
to the Declaration of Rights, Agricultural Land, 
Presidential Term Limits and Tenure. 
Referendums Act [Chapter 2:10] 
 
Voter eligibility: Any registered voter or person entitled 
to register may vote. 
Questions: Must allow a clear "Yes" or "No" answer. 
Result: Passes only if approved by a majority of votes 
cast. 
 
Electoral Act [Chapter 2:13] 
 
The Electoral Act governs the conduct of elections and referendums, conferring authority on the Zimbabwe 
Electoral Commission (ZEC) to administer all aspects of the referendum process — from voter registration and 
polling to the certification and announcement of results. 
 
2013 Constitutional Referendum Precedent 
 
Voters' Roll was not required (valid ID card sufficed) Result was 94.5% "YES" 
 
The 2013 Constitutional Referendum was held under the Referendums Act and produced an overwhelming 
endorsement of the new Constitution. No voters' roll was required; any citizen with a valid national identity card 
could vote.

--- Page 2 ---
Step-by-Step Process of a Referendum 
1 Draft the Constitutional Amendment Bill Initiated by the Executive (Cabinet) or Parliamentarians 
 
2 
Gazette the Bill 
Published in the Government Gazette — requires a 90-day waiting period for public scrutiny, 
stakeholder consultations and parliamentary committee hearings. 
 
3 
Public Consultations 
Conducted by Portfolio Committees — includes public hearings nationwide, civil society input and 
expert submissions. 
 
4 Parliamentary Approval Must pass by a 2/3 majority in the National Assembly AND a 2/3 majority in the Senate. 
 
5 
Presidential Proclamation of Referendum Date 
The President proclaims a referendum date. The referendum is conducted by the Zimbabwe Electoral 
Commission (ZEC). 
 
6 Referendum Campaign Period Equal opportunity principles apply — Yes and No campaigns are held during this period. 
 
7 Conduct of the Referendum National vote by registered voters. The majority (50% + 1) determines the outcome. 
 
8 Certification of Results by ZEC ZEC certifies the results. YES majority → amendment proceeds. NO majority → amendment fails. 
 
9 Presidential Assent Granted only after both parliamentary approval and referendum approval have been secured. 
 
10 Amendment Becomes Law The constitutional amendment is enacted and takes full legal effect.

--- Page 3 ---
Constitutional Legality Tests Applied When Conducting Referendums 
# Constitutional Test 
1 Constitutional Supremacy Test 
2 Procedural Validity Test — Section 328 Compliance 
3 Entrenchment — Mandatory Referendum Requirement 
4 Non-Retrospectivity / Incumbency Benefit Test 
5 Substantive Constitutionalism Test 
6 Public Participation Test 
7 Good Faith Test

tracked_topics.summary: 1.0 INTRODUCTION The Private Voluntary Organisations Amendment Bill was published in the Gazette on the 1st of March 2024. The objectives of the bill are to comply with the Financial Action Taskforce (FATF) recommendations made to Zimbabwe. Further, the Bill is meant to streamline administrative procedures for private voluntary organisations to allow for their efficient regulation and registration. The Bill aims to ensure that private voluntary organisations do not undertake political lobbying as well as involved in the financing of the terrorist and money laundering activities. 2.0 BACKGROUND FATF is an Intergovernmental organisation founded in 1989 on the initiative of the G7 countries. Its main objective is to develop policies to combat money laundering and Zimbabwe is a member. Each member country is assessed periodically for compliance with the policies and legislation on money laundering1 and financing of terrorism. Countries are assessed on two major criteria which are technical compliance and effectiveness.
