tracked_topics.full_content:
--- Page 1 ---
Policy Brief 1 of 2026 
RESEARCH DEPARTMENT 
The Role of the Security Sector in Climate Change Adaptation and Disaster Response in 
Zimbabwe: A Framework for Civil-Military Coordination 
 
 
Chimanikire Soccicah (Researcher) 
 
Executive Summary 
Climate-induced disasters, cyclones, floods, and droughts are increasingly becoming non-
traditional security threats in Zimbabwe. These threats undermine national stability, food 
security, and public safety. Zimbabwe currently lacks a binding legal framework to formally 
integrate the security sector into disaster management although they are often engaged in 
disaster management. Cabinet endorsed the National Multi-Hazard Contingency Plan 
(2025/2026) in December 2025, formally integrating the Zimbabwe Defence Forces (ZDF) 
into disaster management. The plan lacks the legislative force. While the ZDF has introduced 
advanced training and maintains air mobility assets, serious implementation gaps remain: 
resource constraints, over-centralisation in Harare, and concerns that military deployment may 
lean toward enforcement rather than humanitarian support. Drawing on regional models from 
Mozambique, Malawi, and South Africa, this brief advocates for urgent legislative and 
operational reforms, chief among them the enactment of the new Disaster Risk Management 
and Civil Protection Bill, mandated training for police and prison services, dedicated 
engineering and air mobility units, binding standard operating procedures, a joint civil-military 
coordination centre, and contingency funding, to transform the security sector into a 
predictable, accountable partner in climate adaptation while safeguarding civilian authority.

--- Page 2 ---
1.0 Introduction 
Zimbabwe faces escalating climate-related hazards. Cyclone Idai (2019) claimed over 300 
lives, displaced thousands and caused more than USD 600 million in damages. The 2023–2024 
El Niño-induced drought reduced maize harvests by 60 per cent, threatening food security for 
over 7 million rural inhabitants. In response, the government adopted the National 
Multi-Hazard Contingency Plan (2025/2026) in December 2025, formally activating the ZDF’s 
role in responding to projected floods, severe storms and droughts. Drawing lessons from Idai, 
the plan shifts from a purely reactive, top-down approach to a proactive model, with the 
military playing key roles in search and rescue, logistics and disaster risk management training. 
Advanced technologies are being piloted: drone-based mapping of high-risk areas, satellite 
early warning systems and blockchain-based aid distribution to reduce corruption and delays. 
Regional cooperation through the SADC Humanitarian and Emergency Operations Centre is 
also strengthening. 
Despite these advances, major obstacles continue to hamper progress. The current response 
system is marked by high-level policy centralisation in Harare and persistent resource 
shortages. There are also concerns about the securitisation of disaster management, particularly 
when military deployment involves enforcement measures. Past experiences, such as during 
the COVID-19 pandemic, indicate that military involvement may sometimes lead to punitive, 
enforcement-oriented approaches rather than community-based protection. It is important to 
distinguish between such enforcement roles and humanitarian support functions like search and 
rescue or logistics, which raise fewer human rights concerns. Addressing these gaps requires a 
deliberate policy framework that builds on the 2025/2026 Contingency Plan by adding 
legislative backing, binding protocols and modern technology integration. 
2.0 Background 
Zimbabwe’s vulnerability to climate-induced disasters is acute. The Civil Protection Act 
(Chapter 10:06) establishes the Department of Civil Protection (DCP) under the Ministry of 
Local Government and Public Works as the lead disaster agency, yet the DCP lacks sufficient 
logistical capacity, personnel and rapid reach capabilities. A new National Disaster 
Management Centre is nearing completion, which should improve coordination, but the DCP 
itself estimates that USD 300 million is required for full capacitation. As a result, the Zimbabwe 
Defence Forces (ZDF), the Zimbabwe Republic Police and the Zimbabwe Prison and 
Correctional Services are routinely deployed. The 2025/2026 National Multi-Hazard 
Contingency Plan now formally integrates the ZDF as a key operational partner within the 
National Civil Protection Committee, alongside police, non-governmental organisations and 
relevant line ministries. 
The ZDF has made significant progress in disaster training. The Zimbabwe National Defence 
University offers a Master of Science Degree in Disaster Management, and the ZDF unveiled 
a comprehensive disaster management package in 2022, including a 14-week course for 
battalion commanders specifically tailored to disaster response. Training continues through 
live action drills and lessons learned from cyclones and other emergencies. However, these 
programmes are not yet mandated for the police and prison services, and interagency joint 
exercises remain rare. The Air Force of Zimbabwe operates a modest fleet, providing 
substantial air mobility for rapid deployment and resupply, though economic pressures and 
reliance on ageing equipment constrain operational readiness. Section 213 of the Constitution

--- Page 3 ---
clearly empowers the President to deploy the Defence Forces in support of civilian authorities 
during an emergency or disaster. 
Despite all these efforts, operationalisation remains hampered by underfunding, fuel shortages 
and delayed activation protocols. During Cyclone Idai, military helicopters arrived 72 hours 
after landfall due to unclear command channels, a gap that the new contingency plan attempts 
to address. However, without binding standard operating procedures, delays persist. Regional 
neighbours have progressed further. Mozambique’s Armed Forces pre-position troops, Malawi 
maintains a dedicated disaster response battalion, and South Africa’s National Defence Force 
operates a Joint Tactical Headquarters for disasters. Zimbabwe’s contingency plan is a positive 
step, but it lacks legislative backing and detailed interagency protocols. 
Despite these provisions, the law remains incomplete where it matters most: defining who does 
what, when, and under whose authority. The Zimbabwe Defence Forces Act (Chapter 11:02) 
mandates the ZDF to assist civil authorities in emergencies but does not define what constitutes 
an emergency or outline command relationships. The Civil Protection Act similarly omits the 
roles of the security sector. Consequently, integrated climate disaster training modules are 
absent from ordinary police or prison curricula, although military higher education has 
advanced in this area. These deficits translate into preventable loss of life and prolonged 
recovery periods. 
3.0 Legislative and Policy Framework 
The Civil Protection Act (Chapter 10:06), enacted in 1989 and last amended in 2001, remains 
Zimbabwe’s primary disaster management law. It centralises authority in the DCP but does not 
recognise climate change as a distinct hazard category nor mandate security sector integration. 
The government is now developing a more comprehensive Disaster Risk Management and 
Civil Protection Bill to replace the 1989 Act entirely. This was confirmed by the Ministry of 
Local Government in February 2026, and the new Bill aims to address modern threats such as 
droughts and enhance national capacity to prevent and reduce risks. Civil society, including 
ActionAid Zimbabwe, has called for timely finalisation of the Bill. A proposed Civil Protection 
Amendment Bill (2022) has remained pending, but the shift towards a full replacement Bill 
represents significant progress. 
The National Multi-Hazard Contingency Plan (2025/2026), endorsed by Cabinet, now provides 
an operational framework that formally integrates the ZDF. It represents a proactive shift, but 
it is not a legislative instrument. The National Climate Policy of 2017 acknowledges disaster 
risk reduction but defers to the Department of Civil Protection without detailing security sector 
functions. The Zimbabwe Defence Forces Act (Chapter 11:02) provides vague authority. While 
Section 213 of the Constitution already enables deployment, no subordinate legislation 
specifies activation thresholds, cost reimbursement or deactivation procedures. 
Overlapping mandates create confusion: during the 2024 drought, the DCP, Environmental 
Management Agency, ZDF and NGOs all conducted separate assessments without a unified 
command. Reforms must prioritise either amending the Civil Protection Act or passing the new 
Disaster Risk Management Bill to give legal force to the contingency plan’s provisions. 
Legislation should designate the security sector as a formal disaster response pillar with defined 
roles for the ZDF, ZRP and ZPCS. It should mandate annual joint simulations, establish a joint 
civil-military disaster coordination centre, and require climate-disaster modules in all security

--- Page 4 ---
sector training curricula, building on the ZDF’s existing programmes. Without these legislative 
changes, the 2025/2026 Contingency Plan remains a well-intentioned but unenforceable 
roadmap. 
4.0 Lessons for Zimbabwe from Regional Best Practices 
Mozambique, Malawi and South Africa have successfully integrated security sectors into 
disaster management through legislative mandates, dedicated units and binding protocols. 
• Mozambique formalised civil-military disaster cooperation following Cyclone Idai 
(2019) via Decree No. 78/2020, creating Provincial Disaster Management Committees 
with military voting powers. The Armed Forces (FADM) now pre-position engineering 
and medical units in cyclone-prone provinces, reducing response times from 72 to under 
12 hours. 
• Malawi established the Malawi Defence Force Disaster Response Battalion in 2018. 
This 800-person unit is trained in flood rescue, field hospital setup and aerial logistics. 
It operates under a joint command with the Department of Disaster Management Affairs 
through a signed memorandum of understanding. Between 2019 and 2023, this unit 
reduced flood mortality by 40 per cent. 
• South Africa institutionalised civil-military coordination through the Disaster 
Management Act (2002, amended 2015), mandating the SANDF to establish a Joint 
Tactical Headquarters for each declared disaster, with compulsory annual joint 
exercises. 
For Zimbabwe, these models demonstrate that a contingency plan alone is insufficient. Three 
pillars are required: (1) a legislative mandate clarifying roles and activation procedures; (2) 
dedicated units with climate-disaster specialisation; and (3) binding protocols (MoUs or SOPs) 
negotiated pre-disaster. Parliament should mandate the DCP, Ministry of Defence and Ministry 
of Local Government to negotiate a tripartite framework agreement within 12 months, building 
on the 2025/2026 Contingency Plan. 
5.0 Policy Options 
5.1. Specialised Climate-Disaster Training for All Security Forces 
Integrate climate change adaptation, disaster response and civil-military coordination modules 
into ZRP and ZPCS training curricula. Training for police and prisons should include 
hydrological forecasting, shelter management, contamination control, humanitarian principles 
and drone operation. Initial costs include curriculum development and train-the-trainer 
programmes. Benefits include faster, more professional responses and reduced civil-military 
friction. 
5.2. Dedicated Disaster Response Engineering and Air Mobility Units 
Establish a permanent ZDF Engineering Company (bridge construction, debris clearance, 
water purification) and augment existing air assets. While substantial capital and annual 
operating costs would be needed for specialised engineering equipment, fuel and maintenance, 
the benefits would be considerable: response times reduced from days to hours and access to 
remote districts such as Chimanimani, Binga and Mbire.

--- Page 5 ---
5.3. Advanced Technology Integration (Drones, GIS, Blockchain) 
Scale up the government’s drone pilot programme for high-risk area mapping and real-time 
damage assessment. Establish a National Disaster Geospatial Intelligence Unit within the DCP, 
staffed by ZDF geospatial analysts. Use blockchain-based aid tracking to prevent diversion and 
ensure transparency. Costs would include the acquisition of drones, GIS software and 
associated training. Benefits would include faster situational awareness, improved resource 
allocation and reduced corruption. 
5.4. Civil-Military Coordination Protocols (SOPs) 
Draft and mandate standard operating procedures for civil-military disaster response, covering: 
activation triggers (e.g., presidential declaration or DCP request), command and control 
(civilian-led with military liaison), resource reimbursement (national treasury to cover military 
costs), information sharing (joint situation rooms) and deactivation procedures. Development 
costs would be incurred, but the benefits include eliminated ambiguity, faster authorisation and 
accountability, directly addressing concerns over militarisation and centralised control. 
5.5. Enact the Disaster Risk Management and Civil Protection Bill 
Parliament should prioritise finalising and passing the new Disaster Risk Management and 
Civil Protection Bill, which replaces the outdated Civil Protection Act. The Bill should 
formally designate the security sector as a disaster response pillar, define specific ZDF, ZRP 
and ZPCS functions, mandate pre-positioning of assets during hazard seasons, and require 
annual joint simulations with civilian agencies. This would give legal force to the 2025/2026 
Contingency Plan and align with Section 213 of the Constitution. Costs would include 
parliamentary drafting and stakeholder validation. Benefits would include legal clarity, 
sustained political will and eligibility for international disaster response funding. 
5.6. Establish a Joint Civil-Military Disaster Coordination Centre 
Create a permanent, interagency coordination centre hosted by the DCP and co-staffed by the 
ZDF to maintain asset inventories, conduct risk mapping, facilitate pre-season planning and 
manage real-time information during emergencies. While initial setup costs would be required 
to cover communications, GIS systems and staffing, with additional annual running costs, the 
benefits include unified command, reduced duplication and institutional memory across 
disaster cycles, countering the current overcentralisation in Harare. 
5.7. Pre-Positioning and Contingency Funding 
Authorise the Ministry of Finance to allocate a dedicated annual contingency fund enabling 
pre-positioning of food, fuel, medical supplies and engineering stores in high-risk provinces 
(Manicaland, Masvingo, Matabeleland South). Benefits include self-sufficiency, reducing 
reliance on delayed NGO supplies, and faster first response within 6 to 12 hours of disaster 
onset. 
6.0 Recommendations 
Parliament should: 
• Enact the Disaster Risk Management and Civil Protection Bill to replace the Civil 
Protection Act (Chapter 10:06), giving legislative force to the 2025/2026 National

--- Page 6 ---
Multi-Hazard Contingency Plan, formally integrating the security sector and defining 
roles, activation criteria and command relationships, consistent with Section 213 of the 
Constitution. 
• Mandate specialised climate-disaster training for ZRP and ZPCS personnel, building 
on the ZDF’s existing MSc in Disaster Management and 14-week battalion commander 
course, and require annual joint simulations with civilian agencies. 
• Allocate resources for dedicated engineering units and ensure that the Air Force’s 
existing helicopters are properly fuelled and maintained for disaster response, 
acknowledging operational constraints from ageing equipment. 
• Adopt binding civil-military coordination protocols (SOPs) negotiated between the 
DCP, Ministry of Defence and Ministry of Local Government, addressing securitisation 
concerns by distinguishing enforcement roles from humanitarian support and clarifying 
civilian authority. 
• Establish a permanent Joint Civil-Military Disaster Coordination Centre to 
operationalise interagency planning, real-time response and advanced technology 
integration (drones, GIS, blockchain). 
• Create a contingency fund for pre-positioned disaster assets in climate-vulnerable 
provinces, managed jointly by the DCP and ZDF. 
• mandate the Zimbabwe Human Rights Commission to receive and investigate 
complaints of military overreach during disaster responses, with a 30-day reporting 
requirement 
7.0 Conclusion 
Climate-induced disasters are no longer exceptional events but recurring national security 
threats. Zimbabwe has taken important steps with the National Multi-Hazard Contingency Plan 
(2025/2026) and the development of the Disaster Risk Management and Civil Protection Bill. 
The ZDF possesses constitutional authority under Section 213, substantial air assets, and 
advanced training capacity. However, a plan without legislative backing, binding protocols and 
adequate funding remains fragile. Persistent challenges, resource shortages, centralised control 
and risks of militarisation must be addressed through the reforms outlined above. Short-term 
measures, including specialised training for police and prison services, binding SOPs, 
contingency funding and drone and GIS integration, combined with long-term legislative 
enactment, can transform the ZDF, ZRP and ZPCS into effective, accountable disaster response 
partners. Failure to act will perpetuate preventable suffering, economic loss and erosion of 
public trust. Parliament must lead the urgent process of integrating the security sector into 
climate adaptation, ensuring that those who defend the nation also protect it from the rising 
tides of climate change. 
(Disclaimer: The views expressed in this brief belong solely to the author and do not 
necessarily reflect the position of Parliament of Zimbabwe.)

--- Page 7 ---

Management and Civil Protection Bill: Policy Brief. Harare: MoLGPW

--- Page 1 ---
BLESSING CHIWANZA 1 
 
 
Policy Brief 1/2026: 
Zero-Rating vs VAT Exemption: Policy Choices for 
Industrial Competitiveness in Zimbabwe 
 
Executive Summary 
Zimbabwe’s industrialisation agenda, 
anchored in Vision 2030, is being 
constrained by persistently high production 
costs, low-capacity utilisation, and heavy 
reliance on imported inputs. The structure 
of the Value Added Tax (VAT) system 
particularly the distinction between zero-
rating and VAT exemption has emerged as a 
critical policy lever with direct implications 
for industrial performance. 
While both instruments aim to reduce the 
tax burden, their economic effects differ 
significantly. Zero-rating allows firms to 
reclaim input VAT, thereby lowering 
production costs and preserving 
competitiveness. VAT exemption, by 
contrast, prevents input tax recovery and 
embeds VAT into production costs. 
Current expansions in VAT exemptions risk 
increasing the cost of production at a time 
when Zimbabwe’s industrial capacity 
utilisation remains below optimal levels 
and firms continue to rely heavily on 
imported inputs. 
This approach may unintentionally weaken 
domestic manufacturing and slow industrial 
recovery. 
This brief recommends a strategic shift 
toward expanded zero-rating of productive 
inputs, supported by reforms to VAT refund 
administration, in order to reduce costs, 
support value addition, and enhance 
competitiveness.

--- Page 2 ---
BLESSING CHIWANZA 2 
 
Introduction 
Industrial Competitiveness and VAT 
Policy 
Zimbabwe’s industrial sector continues to 
operate below potential, constrained by 
high input costs, foreign currency 
shortages, and competition from imports. 
Manufacturing firms rely significantly on 
imported raw materials, making them 
highly sensitive to tax policy on imports. 
VAT, governed by the Value Added Tax Act 
[Chapter 23:12], is levied on goods and 
services as well as imports. While designed 
to be neutral, its impact depends on how 
goods are classified within the system. 
VAT policy is therefore not merely a 
revenue instrument it directly influences 
production costs, pricing structures, and 
investment decisions. Poorly designed VAT 
measures can raise costs and discourage 
local production, while well-designed 
measures can support industrial growth and 
competitiveness. 
Zero-Rating vs VAT Exemption: The 
Policy Distinction 
The VAT Act provides two mechanisms for 
tax relief: 
Section 10 (Zero-Rating): Supplies are 
taxed at 0%, allowing firms to reclaim input 
VAT. 
Section 11 (Exemption): Supplies are not 
taxed, but firms cannot recover input VAT. 
Zero-rating preserves VAT neutrality by 
ensuring that taxation does not increase 
production costs along the value chain. VAT 
exemption, however, results in embedded 
tax costs, effectively increasing the cost of 
production. 
Failure to maintain VAT neutrality raises 
production costs, distorts pricing, and 
weakens competitiveness, particularly in 
import-dependent manufacturing sectors. 
Economic Implications for Zimbabwean 
Industry 
For Zimbabwean manufacturers, the 
distinction between zero-rating and VAT 
exemption has direct implications for 
production costs and competitiveness. 
Under a zero-rating regime, firms are able 
to recover VAT paid on inputs, thereby 
lowering their cost base and improving 
their pricing competitiveness in both 
domestic and export markets. In contrast, 
VAT exemption prevents the recovery of 
input tax, effectively converting VAT into a 
cost of production, which increases 
operating expenses, compresses margins, 
and raises final prices. Evidence from the 
International Growth Centre indicates that 
VAT exemptions raise the effective tax 
burden on firms by embedding

--- Page 3 ---
BLESSING CHIWANZA 3 
 
unrecoverable input VAT, particularly in 
manufacturing sectors, while Warwick et al. 
(2022) show that such regimes distort 
supply chains and reduce productivity. In 
Zimbabwe, these effects are intensified by 
high dependence on imported raw 
materials, persistent foreign currency 
constraints, and limited domestic 
production of intermediate goods. As a 
result, VAT exemption policies risk 
increasing production costs at a time when 
industrial recovery depends on improving 
efficiency, reducing input costs, and 
strengthening competitiveness. 
Administrative Efficiency and 
Implementation Constraints 
Although VAT exemption is often perceived 
as administratively simpler, it introduces 
classification ambiguities and increases 
opportunities for tax avoidance, particularly 
where distinctions between exempt and 
taxable goods are unclear. Zero-rating is 
more consistent with efficient VAT design 
but depends on a well-functioning refund 
system to ensure that firms can recover 
input VAT in a timely manner. 
In Zimbabwe, delays in VAT refunds 
continue to impose significant liquidity 
constraints on businesses, particularly in 
manufacturing, effectively tying up 
working capital and increasing the cost of 
financing operations. Addressing this 
challenge requires targeted administrative 
reforms within the Zimbabwe Revenue 
Authority, including the digitisation of 
refund processes, enforcement of time-
bound refund periods, and strengthening of 
institutional capacity. Improving refund 
efficiency is therefore critical to ensuring 
that zero-rating delivers its intended 
benefits and supports industrial activity. 
Comparative Insights from Peer 
Economies 
Experiences from peer economies in Africa 
demonstrate the limitations of VAT 
exemptions as a tool for supporting 
industrial development. In South Africa, the 
Davis Tax Committee found that 
exemptions often resulted in inefficiencies 
and poor targeting, reducing their 
effectiveness. Studies in Ghana and 
Ethiopia similarly show that VAT 
exemptions increase production costs, 
encourage informality, and weaken tax 
compliance. In contrast, countries that have 
prioritised VAT neutrality through zero-
rating have achieved better outcomes in 
terms of industrial competitiveness, supply 
chain efficiency, and formal sector 
participation. Evidence from Warwick et al. 
(2022) further indicates that replacing VAT 
exemptions with more neutral policy 
instruments improves both efficiency and 
equity outcomes. These findings highlight

--- Page 4 ---
BLESSING CHIWANZA 4 
 
that VAT policy design plays a critical role 
in shaping industrial performance and 
should be aligned with broader economic 
development objectives. 
Policy Options 
Option A: Maintain the Current VAT 
Structure 
Retain the existing mix of zero-rating and 
VAT exemptions. This provides short-term 
relief but continues to raise production 
costs and weaken industrial 
competitiveness. 
Option B: Replace VAT Relief with 
Targeted Subsidies 
Use direct subsidies or transfers instead of 
VAT adjustments. Allows precise targeting 
but is fiscally demanding and 
administratively complex to implement at 
scale. 
Option B: Expand Zero-Rating for 
Strategic Inputs (Preferred Option) 
Extend zero-rating to cover all strategic raw 
materials and intermediate goods used in 
key industrial and agricultural value chains. 
This has an impact of reducing production 
costs, enhances competitiveness, and 
supports value addition, but requires 
improved VAT refund administration. 
 
Recommendations 
1. Parliament should amend the Value 
Added Tax Act [Chapter 23:12] to expand 
the zero-rating schedule to include all 
strategic raw materials and intermediate 
inputs in manufacturing and agriculture. 
2. The Ministry of Finance, Economic 
Development and Investment Promotion 
should conduct a comprehensive review of 
VAT exemptions and implement a phased 
transition toward zero-rating for productive 
inputs. 
3. The Zimbabwe Revenue Authority 
should modernise VAT refund systems 
through digitalisation and enforce statutory 
timeframes for refunds to improve business 
liquidity. 
4. The Ministry of Industry and Commerce 
should integrate VAT policy into the 
National Industrial Development Policy by 
identifying priority sectors requiring zero-
rated inputs. 
5. The Ministry of Finance, in collaboration 
with ZIMSTAT, should establish a 
monitoring framework to assess the impact 
of VAT policy on industrial performance, 
investment, and import substitution.

--- Page 5 ---
BLESSING CHIWANZA 5 
 
Conclusion 
The distinction between zero-rating and 
VAT exemption represents a critical policy 
choice with direct implications for 
Zimbabwe’s industrial competitiveness. 
VAT exemption effectively increases 
production costs by embedding input taxes, 
while zero-rating supports efficiency and 
competitiveness by preserving VAT 
neutrality. 
At a time when Zimbabwe’s industrial 
sector requires cost reduction and 
productivity gains, expanding VAT 
exemptions risks reinforcing structural 
constraints. A strategic shift toward zero-
rating, supported by administrative 
reforms, offers a clear pathway to support 
industrial recovery and long-term economic 
growth. 
Aligning VAT policy with national 
development objectives is therefore 
essential to advancing Zimbabwe’s Vision 
2030 and strengthening the foundations of 
domestic production. 
 
 
 
 
 
References 
1. Government of Zimbabwe (n.d.) Value 
Added Tax Act [Chapter 23:12]. 
Harare: Government of Zimbabwe. 
2. International Growth Centre (2018) 
VAT and Firms in Developing 
Countries. London: International 
Growth Centre. 
3. Warwick, R., Harris, T., Phillips, D. and 
Goldman, M. (2022) ‘The redistributive 
power of VAT exemptions versus cash 
transfers’, World Development, 151.

tracked_topics.full_content:
--- Page 1 ---
Page1 
 
Policy Brief: 
The Future of Burial Space in Zimbabwe – A Growing Land Crisis in 
Urban Areas 
 
 
 
 
Executive Summary 
The increasing number of annual deaths in Zimbabwe is leading to a growing demand for burial spaces, 
putting pressure on available land. Given that many Zimbabweans oppose cremation and the reuse of 
old graves due to cultural and spiritual beliefs, cemeteries are rapidly consuming land that could 
otherwise be used for agriculture and development in urban areas. This policy brief projects the long-
term implications of burial practices on land availability and explores sustainable solutions to balance 
cultural traditions with land conservation. 
 
Introduction 
 As Zimbabwe's population grows and 
urbanization expands, the demand for burial 
space is becoming an unsustainable land use 
issue. Traditional cemeteries are rapidly 
expanding, encroaching on agricultural land 
and limiting future development opportunities. 
This increasing demand for burial sites poses a 
threat to sustainable development and food 
security. Additionally, due to cultural beliefs, 
many Zimbabweans reject cremation and 
cemetery reuse, further exacerbating the need 
for new burial spaces. 
 
Target Audience 
• Parliamentarians and policymakers 
• Urban and rural planners 
• Traditional and religious leaders 
 
Objective of the Policy Brief 
To project the impact of burial space 
consumption in Zimbabwe. 
 
Cultural and Religious Beliefs on Burial 
Practices 
Cultural and religious traditions in Zimbabwe 
strongly influence burial practices. Cremation 
is widely rejected due to beliefs in ancestral 
spirits and deep respect for the deceased. Many 
fear that disturbing human remains may bring 
misfortune, making exhumation or grave reuse 
unacceptable. Additionally, communities 
oppose repurposing cemetery land for 
agriculture or development, as gravesites hold 
profound spiritual significance. These beliefs 
make it challenging to introduce alternative 
burial methods despite growing land shortages. 
Evidence Analysis

--- Page 2 ---
Page2 
Annual Death Registrations and Projected 
Burial Space Needs 
According to the Zimbabwe National Statistics 
Agency (ZIMSTAT), the number of deaths 
registered annually has risen due to factors such 
as disease outbreaks, road accidents, and 
natural causes. The following data from 2020 -
2024 shows the number of deaths per year: 
• 2020: 126,360 deaths 
• 2021: 138,736 deaths 
• 2022: 124,999 deaths 
• 2023: 124,412 deaths 
• 2024: 124,718 deaths 
Source: https://database.earth/population/zimbabwe/deaths 
 
Considering the five-year average of 
127,845 deaths per year, with each grave 
requiring 3 square meters, the annual land 
consumption for burials amounts to 
383,535 square meters. This growing 
demand for burial space raises concerns 
about sustainable land use, particularly as 
urban areas expand and available land 
becomes increasingly scarce. As the 
population continues to grow, the burial 
rate is expected to rise, placing pressure on 
land resources especially in urban areas. 
The following Figure 1 presents a 
projection of deaths from 2025 to 2100, 
highlighting the increasing need for burial 
space planning and alternative solutions. 
Figure 1: Future Population Deaths In 
Zimbabwe (2025-2100). 
 
 
 
Source: https://dtabase.earth/population/zimbabwe/deaths 
 
As the burial rate is projected to rise annually to 
352,325 burials, the demand for burial land will 
increase correspondingly. 
 
 With an initial estimate of 125,303 burials 
annually, and each individual requiring 3 
square meters of land, the total burial space 
consumed per year amounts to 375,909 square 
meters. At this higher rate, the total land 
required per year would surge to 1,056,975 
square meters. This growing need for burial 
space highlights the pressing concern of land 
allocation and long-term planning for 
cemeteries, particularly as Zimbabwe faces an 
ever-expanding population and the inevitability 
of mortality. 
 
Policy Options and Recommendations 
1. Introduce vertical burial structures to minimize land use. 
2. Provide incentives for voluntary cremation while respecting cultural sensitivities. 
3. Educate communities on sustainable burial practices. 
Conclusion 
Zimbabwe faces a burial space crisis due to population growth, urbanization, and cultural resistance to 
alternative burial methods. As cemeteries consume increasing amounts of agricultural land, 
policymakers must act now to ensure culturally appropriate and sustainable burial solutions. Sustainable 
alternatives, such as cremation and vertical cemeteries, must be explored. 
 
References 
• Zimbabwe National Statistics Agency (ZIMSTAT) Reports, 2020–2023 
• Moyo, T. (2022). "Urban Cemetery Challenges in Zimbabwe: A Case Study of Harare." 
• Chikowore, P. & Dube, R. (2021). "Cultural Perspectives on Cremation and Burial Practices 
in Zimbabwe." 
• Government of Zimbabwe, Ministry of Local Government and Public Works Policy Reports 
(2023). 
• https://database.earth/population/zimbabwe/deaths
